parts.intro: You will hear a woman phoning an adult learning centre to ask about a language course.

turns.text: Good morning, Northgate Adult Learning Centre, Tom speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hi there. I'm ringing about your language courses. I saw that the new term starts soon, and I wondered if there were still any places left.
There are on most of them, yes. Shall I take a few details first, and then I can tell you what's available at your level?
Sure, that's fine.
Can I have your name, please?
It's Margaret Haverley. That's Mrs.
And is that H-A-V-E-R-L-Y?
Nearly. There's an E before the Y. So it's H-A-V-E-R-L-E-Y.
Got it, thanks. And which language are you interested in?
Well, I was originally thinking of Italian, because I went to Rome last spring and absolutely loved it. But actually, I've decided on Portuguese.
Portuguese, OK. Can I ask why you'd like to learn it? It just helps us put people in the right group.

Of course. My daughter married a man from Lisbon, and they've got two little boys now. They speak mostly Portuguese at home, and I'd really love to be able to chat with my grandchildren when I visit. At the moment I just smile and nod.
That's a lovely reason. Have you studied any Portuguese before?
A little. I've been using one of those language apps on my phone. I'd say about six months... no, actually it's longer than that. I started in March, so it's closer to eight months now.
Eight months, that's useful. So you probably wouldn't want the complete beginners' group.
Probably not. I know quite a lot of words, but I can't really put a sentence together when someone actually speaks to me.
That's very common with apps. And do you have a preference for when you study? All our language classes are on weekday evenings.
Tuesday would have been ideal, but...
I'm afraid the Tuesday group for Portuguese filled up last week. There's a Thursday group, though, and that still has three places.
Thursday's fine. I play tennis on Mondays and Wednesdays, so it suits me better anyway.
Great, I'll put you down for that. And just for our records, how did you find out about us? Was it through our website?
I did look at the website afterwards, but the first thing I saw was a leaflet that someone had left in the waiting room at my doctor's surgery.
Oh good, those are new this term, so it's nice to know they're working.
Right, so let me tell you about the options for Portuguese at your level.
Yes, please.
The main one is the standard evening course. That runs for ten weeks, two hours every Thursday, from seven until nine.
And what does that cost?
The fee is one hundred and eighty-five pounds. You might see two hundred and ten on the website, but that's the price if you also want us to order the course book for you.
I see. So the 185 is just for the lessons.

That's right. And something people really like is included in the fee: a conversation club. It meets once a month on a Saturday morning, and there's always a native speaker there, so you get some real practice.
That sounds like exactly what I need. What about the book, then? Do I have to order it through you?

No, you don't. Lots of students buy it themselves. It isn't sold in ordinary bookshops, but you can get it from the college shop, on the ground floor next to the café, and it's a bit cheaper there than ordering it through us.
Oh, good. And is there anything I need to bring to the first lesson?
Just a passport photo. We use it for your student card, which gets you into the building in the evenings and gives you a small discount in the café.
Not a copy of my passport or anything like that?
No, only the photo. Your enrolment form is enough for identification.
Lovely. Well, I think I'd like to book the Thursday group, then.
Wonderful. I'll email you the enrolment form this afternoon.

parts.intro: You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to a science museum.

turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Science Museum. I'm Helen, and I'll be looking after your group this morning. To start with, I'll tell you a little about the history of this building, and then I'll explain where everything is.

Now, a lot of visitors assume that this building used to be a railway station, probably because of the big clock tower above the entrance. In fact, it was built in 1902 as a power station, and for nearly sixty years it produced the electricity for the city's trams. The enormous space in the middle, which we call the Turbine Hall, is where the generators once stood.

There are a couple of changes this year that you may have heard about. You might have read that we're opening an observatory on the roof. That is happening, but not until next spring, I'm afraid. And entry for children under sixteen has always been free here, so nothing has changed there. What is new is that on Fridays we now stay open late, until nine o'clock in the evening, with talks and live demonstrations for adults.

The most popular gallery by far is the Flight Gallery on the first floor. Most people head straight there when we open, so it's packed in the morning, and the school groups usually come back to it just before closing time. Your best chance of having it almost to yourself is straight after lunch, between about one and two. And if you're hoping to eat in the café, it gets very busy at midday, so you might like to have an early lunch first and then go up to the gallery.

A quick word about photography. You're very welcome to take photos and videos anywhere in the museum, including the special exhibitions. The only thing we ask is that you don't use flash, because the light gradually damages some of the older paper documents and photographs on display.

Right, if you look at the ground-floor plan in your leaflet, I'll point out some of the key places. We're at the main entrance now, which you'll find along the bottom edge of the plan, and directly ahead of you is the ticket desk.

If you have large bags or coats, the cloakroom is immediately to your left as you come in, so it's the room right next to the entrance on that side. Don't go into the room in the corner beyond it; that's the staff room.

On the other side of the entrance, there are two rooms. The first one, right beside the entrance, is our first-aid room. The gift shop is the one beyond it, in the corner of the building, so you'll pass it on your way out.

Now, walk past the ticket desk and you'll find yourselves in the Turbine Hall. Go all the way to the far end of the hall, and you'll see a wide doorway in the middle of the north wall. Go through that doorway and you're in the Planetarium. Shows start every half hour.

Families with young children usually love the Water Lab, where you can build dams and control a model river. To get there, take the door on the west side of the Turbine Hall, that's the left-hand side as you walk in, and the Water Lab is the large room directly in front of you. The smaller room above it, next to the toilets, is the education office, which isn't open to the public.
If you need to get up to the Flight Gallery and you'd rather not use the stairs, the lifts are on the east side of the Turbine Hall, exactly opposite the Water Lab.
And finally, the Robot Workshop. It's quite easy to miss. It's the small room tucked between the Planetarium and the café, in the top right-hand part of the building. You enter it from the café side.
OK, that's everything. Enjoy your visit, and do come and find me at the ticket desk if you have any questions.

parts.intro: You will hear two students, Chloe and Ryan, discussing their presentation on urban trees with their tutor.

turns.text: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk through your presentation on urban trees before next week?
Yes, thanks for seeing us, Dr Morrison. We've got most of it drafted, but there are a few things we're not sure about.
Fine. Remind me first, why did you choose this topic? It wasn't one of the ones on my list.

No, it wasn't. We did look at your list, but none of them really grabbed us. Then last summer the council cut down all the old plane trees on my street because of some roadworks, and within a few weeks the whole road felt different. Hotter, noisier. So that's really where it started.
And we thought there'd be loads of research on it, but actually there's less than we expected, at least for cities like ours.
That's often the way. Now, you ran a survey of residents. How did that go?

Well, the number of replies was fine. We got about a hundred and forty, which is more than we needed. The trouble was one of the questions. We asked people how they felt about the tree canopy in their street, and it turned out lots of them thought canopy meant the awnings over the shops.
Ah. So some of those answers aren't really usable.
Exactly. We've had to leave that question out of the analysis. Everything else was quick to process, though.
OK. Let's talk about your temperature data. You're using readings from the council's street sensors?
Yes. We wondered whether we should compare the streets with the park as well.

I wouldn't bother. The park isn't really the point, and the council sensors are perfectly reliable. What you're missing is the night. At the moment you've only got daytime readings, but streets with trees stay cooler after dark too, and that matters a lot for people's health, especially older people trying to sleep in a heatwave. You need to include those.
Right, that's easy enough. The sensors record all day and night.
And was there anything in the survey that surprised you?
For me, it was the shopkeepers. I expected them to complain about falling leaves and trees hiding their signs, but most of them actually wanted more trees, not fewer.
What I'd expected, and what we found, was that older residents were the most positive. So that wasn't really a surprise.
And how are you going to finish?
We'd thought about ending with a short video of the street before and after the trees came down.
You've only got fifteen minutes, remember.
That's what I said. And we don't want to just finish with questions; everyone does that. I think we should end with a short list of recommendations for the council.
Yes, OK, I agree. Recommendations it is.
Now, how many benefits of street trees are you going to cover? You can't do everything in fifteen minutes.
We'd listed five. Cooling, flooding, air quality, property values and noise.
Too many. Which do you have the best evidence for?
Air quality, I thought, but when we read more, the studies really disagree. Some trees actually trap pollution at street level.
And we haven't got any figures on house prices, so property values would just be guesswork.

Noise is real, but the effect is quite small. So I'd say we focus on cooling and on flooding. The council's own reports say tree roots and soil soak up a lot of rainwater, and we've got the temperature data for cooling.
Good. Two strong points are much better than five weak ones. Now, let me give you some quick comments on the draft sections you sent me.
Please.
The introduction is far too long. You spend nearly four minutes on the history of street planting in Victorian times. It's interesting, but cut it to one minute at most.
Fair enough.

The survey results section is clear, but it's all in tables. Since you know which street each answer came from, why not show it as a map of the neighbourhood? People would see the pattern immediately.
Oh, that's a nice idea. We could colour the streets.

Exactly. And then the cost comparison, the cost of planting versus the cost of air conditioning and flood repairs. The argument is strong, but some of your figures are from 2009. Prices have changed a lot since then, so look for something more up to date.
OK. I think the council published new figures last year.
Then use those. And your glossary of tree terms at the start, you could move that to the end as a handout. But overall, this is shaping up well.
Thanks, that's really helpful.

parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture about how marine mammals sleep.

turns.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at a question that sounds simple but has puzzled biologists for a long time: how do mammals that live in the sea manage to sleep? For land mammals, sleep is fairly straightforward. You find a safe place, you lie down and you switch off. But whales, dolphins and seals have a problem that we don't. They live in water, but they must come to the surface to breathe. A dolphin that fell deeply asleep in the way that we do would simply drown.

Much of what we first learned came from studies of animals kept in aquariums, where researchers could attach sensors and watch them around the clock. More recently, small tracking devices have allowed us to follow animals in the open ocean, and some of those results have been genuinely surprising.

Let's start with dolphins. As you may know, dolphins rest only one half of the brain at a time, while the other half stays alert, keeping the animal swimming and surfacing to breathe. You can actually see this from the outside, because a resting dolphin closes one eye, the one on the opposite side of the body to the sleeping half of the brain. Every so often the two halves swap over. One remarkable finding concerns newborn calves. For roughly the first month of life, both the calves and their mothers show almost no sign of sleep at all. One explanation is that constant movement helps the young calf to stay warm, but the more widely accepted view is that it protects calves from predators at the stage when they are most vulnerable.

Fur seals are interesting because they sleep in two quite different ways. On land, they sleep very much like land mammals, with both sides of the brain resting together. In the water, however, they switch to dolphin-style sleep, with one half of the brain awake and one front flipper paddling to keep the body in position. And in the water they lose almost all of their REM sleep, which is the stage associated with dreaming in humans. Now, in people, if you are deprived of REM sleep, you make up for it the following night. Researchers expected the seals to do the same when they returned to land. They didn't, and we still don't fully understand why.

Sperm whales provide one of the strangest pictures. In 2008, a research ship drifted by chance into the middle of a group of sperm whales that were completely motionless, hanging in a vertical position just below the surface, heads up. The whales didn't react at all until the ship actually touched one of them. It seems they take short naps of around ten to fifteen minutes in this upright position, and they may sleep less than any other mammal that has been studied.

Sea otters, which spend most of their lives floating on their backs, face a different risk: drifting away from their feeding grounds or out to sea while they rest. Their solution is to wrap themselves in kelp, the long seaweed that grows in coastal forests, which acts rather like an anchor. Groups of otters resting together are known as rafts, and they sometimes hold paws.

Walruses have yet another approach. They are able to sleep in the water by inflating two air sacs in their throat, which keep the head above the surface while the body hangs below, a little like a fishing float. But they are also capable of going without sleep for remarkably long periods. In one study, a walrus was recorded swimming continuously for more than three days without resting at all, and then making up for it with a long sleep on the ice. So rather than following a fixed daily pattern, walruses seem to sleep whenever conditions allow.

Finally, elephant seals. Until recently, nobody knew when these seals slept during their long months at sea. Tracking devices fitted to the seals in California showed that they actually sleep during deep dives, sometimes hundreds of metres below the surface, where they are safer from sharks and killer whales. Some of them turn upside down and spiral slowly downwards, rather like a falling leaf. Altogether, they seem to sleep only about two hours a day while at sea, compared with ten hours or more when they are resting on the beach.

What all of this tells us is that sleep is far more flexible than we once believed. For conservation, it means that protecting quiet resting places matters just as much as protecting feeding grounds. Next week, we'll look at sleep in birds.

texts.title: Island Link Ferries: winter timetable and fares

paragraphs.text: From 1 November to 31 March, Island Link operates a reduced winter service between Porthaven on the mainland and Carrick Island. Crossings take approximately 50 minutes, although journeys may be slower in poor weather.

On weekdays, the first sailing leaves Porthaven at 7.15 and the last returns from Carrick at 18.30. At weekends there are four sailings in each direction, with the first departure from Porthaven at 9.00. Please note that there is no service on 25 December or 1 January.

A single adult foot passenger ticket costs £8.50 and a day return costs £14. Children under five travel free, and children aged five to fifteen pay half the adult fare. Island residents who hold a valid Resident Card receive a 40% discount on all tickets, including vehicle fares. Resident Cards are issued by the island council, not by Island Link.

Tickets can be bought online, through the Island Link app or from the ticket office at either terminal. Tickets bought online or through the app are £1 cheaper than those bought at the terminal. During the winter season, foot passengers do not normally need to book in advance, but all vehicles must be booked at least 24 hours before departure.

Regular travellers may prefer a ten-journey book, which can be shared between members of the same household and remains valid for twelve months from the date of purchase. Ten-journey books are sold only at the terminal ticket offices and cannot be refunded once any journey has been used. A monthly season ticket for commuters is also available on request.

texts.title: Travelling with Island Link: what you need to know

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Luggage. Each passenger may bring up to two large items of luggage free of charge. These should be left in the luggage racks on the car deck before you go up to the passenger lounges. Smaller bags may be taken with you. Please do not leave luggage on the stairs or in the corridors, as these must be kept clear in case the ship has to be evacuated.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Bicycles. Bicycles are carried free of charge, but space is limited to twelve bicycles per sailing, so arrive early in summer. Electric bicycles are welcome, but their batteries may not be charged on board for safety reasons.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Pets. Dogs are welcome on all sailings but must stay on a lead at all times. They are allowed in the outdoor seating areas and in the rear lounge, which is marked with a paw symbol. Assistance dogs may accompany their owners anywhere on the ship. Other pets must travel in a secure carrier.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Vehicles. Drivers should arrive at the terminal at least 30 minutes before departure, or their space may be given to another vehicle. Once the ship has left port, passengers may not return to the car deck until they are asked to do so shortly before arrival.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Accessibility. Both of our ships have lifts between the car deck and the passenger lounges, and accessible toilets on every passenger deck. If you need help boarding, please tell staff at the ticket office when you check in, and a member of the crew will meet you.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Delays and cancellations. In strong winds, sailings may be delayed or cancelled. Up-to-date information is posted on our website and app from 6 a.m. each day. If your sailing is cancelled, you may travel on the next available sailing at no extra cost or request a full refund.

texts.title: First aid at Harbourside Logistics: what every employee needs to know

paragraphs.text: Accidents can happen in any workplace, and a warehouse with moving vehicles, heavy loads and high shelving carries particular risks. This guide explains what to do if you or a colleague is injured or becomes ill at work. Please read it carefully during your first week, and ask your supervisor if anything is unclear.

Every shift has at least two trained first aiders on duty. Their names and photographs are displayed on the noticeboard beside the main clocking-in point, and first aiders also wear a green armband while they are working. If someone is hurt, contact a first aider immediately using the radio channel set aside for emergencies, which is channel 4. Do not try to treat anything more than a very minor injury yourself.

Not every situation involves an obvious injury. If you feel dizzy, faint or unusually unwell while working, stop what you are doing, move away from any machinery or vehicles and tell a colleague. The same applies if you notice that a colleague seems confused or unwell. It is always better to raise a concern that turns out to be unnecessary than to ignore a warning sign.

First aid kits are kept at the end of every aisle and in each delivery vehicle. They are checked every Monday by the duty first aider, but if you use anything from a kit, write it on the form inside the lid so that it can be replaced. Eye-wash stations are located next to the battery-charging area and in the chemical store, because these are the places where splashes are most likely.

If an injury is serious, a first aider or supervisor will call an ambulance. While waiting, someone should be sent to the main gate to direct the ambulance crew, as the site can be confusing for visitors. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger, for example from a vehicle or a fire.

Every accident, however small, must be recorded in the accident book, which is kept in the site office. This includes near misses, where nobody was hurt but someone could have been. Records help the health and safety team spot patterns. For example, a series of minor hand injuries last year led to new gloves being provided for all packing staff.

Harbourside Logistics is always looking for volunteers to train as first aiders, particularly on the night shift, where numbers are lowest. Any permanent employee who has completed their probation period may apply. You do not need any previous medical experience.

Training takes place over three days at an approved training centre during normal working hours, and you will be paid as usual while you attend. At the end of the course there is a practical assessment, and successful candidates receive a certificate that is valid for three years. Before it expires, you will need to attend a two-day refresher course to keep your qualification.

In recognition of the extra responsibility, first aiders receive an additional allowance of £25 per month, paid with their normal salary. They are also given priority when requesting their preferred shifts, as long as at least two first aiders remain on duty at all times.

First aiders are expected to keep their skills up to date. Every six months, the health and safety team organises a short practice session, usually based on a realistic accident scenario, such as a fall from a ladder. Attendance at these sessions is compulsory for all first aiders. Sessions are held at the start of a shift, so nobody needs to come in on a day off, and they rarely last longer than an hour.

If you are interested, speak to your line manager or complete the application form on the staff intranet. Places on each course are limited, and applications are considered in the order in which they are received.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than two centuries, the northern coast has been one of the most dangerous stretches of water in the region. Strong tides, sudden fog and hidden rocks claimed hundreds of ships, many of them small fishing boats and coastal traders carrying coal, timber and grain. The chain of lighthouses that now stands along the coast, from Selsey Point in the west to the Brannock Islands in the east, was built gradually over about a hundred years, and each tower tells part of the story of how engineers learned to tame the sea.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest lights were little more than fires burning in iron baskets on top of stone towers. They were expensive to run, as each one consumed several tonnes of coal every winter, and they were unreliable: in heavy rain the fire could go out, and in strong wind the smoke often hid the flame entirely. Sailors complained that it was sometimes impossible to tell a lighthouse fire from a cottage chimney. By the 1820s, coal fires had been replaced along most of the coast by oil lamps, which burned more steadily and could be placed behind glass. Even so, the early oil lamps had their own drawbacks, since the glass quickly became blackened with soot and had to be cleaned several times every night.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Building the towers themselves was a formidable challenge. Many of the most dangerous rocks lay several kilometres offshore and were only fully above water for a few hours at low tide. At the Garron Rock, construction workers lived for three summers on a supply ship anchored nearby, rowing out whenever the tide allowed. They could sometimes work for only two hours a day. Each granite block was cut and shaped on the mainland, numbered, and then fitted into place on the rock, so that the stones locked together like the pieces of a puzzle. This technique, borrowed from earlier builders elsewhere, allowed the tower to withstand waves that would have destroyed a conventional structure. Even so, the work was dangerous: storms twice swept away the half-finished walls, and on one occasion the supply ship itself was driven onto the rocks, although all of the crew were rescued.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important advance, however, was not in the towers but in the lights. In the middle of the nineteenth century, a new type of lens made from rings of carefully shaped glass began to be installed along the coast. Instead of letting most of the light escape upwards or downwards, the lens gathered it into a powerful horizontal beam. A lamp that had once been visible from perhaps eight kilometres could now be seen from over thirty. For the first time, ships could pick up one light before losing sight of the previous one, and the coast became, in effect, a continuous line of signals. The lenses were costly and fragile, and each one had to be assembled with great precision by specialists who travelled from tower to tower, but the improvement in safety was so obvious that within twenty years almost every light on the coast had been fitted with one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Distance alone was not enough, though. A sailor needed to know not only that there was a lighthouse ahead but which lighthouse it was. The solution was to give each one its own character. Some showed a steady light, while others flashed in a particular pattern, for example two short flashes every ten seconds, or were fitted with coloured glass so that they appeared red when seen from a dangerous direction. These patterns were printed in tables that every ship's officer carried, and a navigator in fog or darkness could identify his position simply by counting. In fog, when even the strongest beam could not be seen, many towers also sounded a horn in a similar coded pattern, so that ships could recognise a lighthouse by ear as well as by eye.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In the twentieth century, electricity, radio signals and eventually satellite navigation reduced the importance of the lights. Between the 1960s and the 1990s, every lighthouse on the coast was converted to automatic operation, controlled and monitored from a centre on the mainland. Some people predicted that the towers would soon be abandoned altogether. In practice, most remain in service, because small boats and yachts, whose electronic equipment can fail, still rely on them, and because a light that can be seen with the naked eye is a reassurance that no screen can quite replace.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Today, the lighthouses are also finding new roles. Several of the former keepers' cottages have been turned into holiday accommodation, and the profits help to pay for maintenance. At Selsey Point, the old engine room is now a small museum, while the tower at Corran Head houses instruments that record wind speed and wave height for weather forecasters. Local groups argue that these uses are essential, since a building that people visit and value is far more likely to be protected. Whatever the future holds, the lighthouses remain a striking reminder of a time when human skill and determination were the only defence against a dangerous sea.

tasks.prompt: You often shop at a large supermarket near your home. You have an idea that you think would improve the service for customers. Write a letter to the manager of the supermarket. In your letter, say how long you have been a customer, describe a problem that customers experience, and explain your idea and how it would help. Write at least 150 words. You do NOT need to write any addresses. Begin your letter as follows: Dear Sir or Madam,

bullets: say how long you have been a customer
describe a problem that customers experience
explain your idea and how it would help

key_features: formal tone throughout and 'Yours faithfully' to match 'Dear Sir or Madam'
clear statement of how long the writer has shopped there
a specific problem with concrete detail (time, example)
a practical suggestion and why it would help customers and the store

model_answer.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I have shopped at your Hillcrest Road branch almost every week for the past six years, and I would like to make a suggestion that I believe would benefit many of your regular customers.

At the moment, the store opens at eight o'clock in the morning and closes at ten at night. However, the busiest period is clearly between five and seven in the evening, when people stop on their way home from work. At that time, there are often only two checkouts open, and the queues regularly stretch back into the aisles. Last Thursday, I waited almost twenty-five minutes simply to pay for a loaf of bread and some milk.

My suggestion is that you open at least two additional checkouts during this early-evening period, or alternatively install several self-service machines near the entrance for customers buying only a few items. I have noticed that a nearby pharmacy introduced self-service tills last year, and its queues have almost disappeared.

I am sure this change would encourage loyal customers like me to keep shopping with you rather than going elsewhere. I would be grateful if you could let me know whether this is something you might consider.

Yours faithfully,
Samira Chowdhury

tasks.prompt: Some people think that museums and art galleries should be free for everyone to visit. Others believe that visitors should pay an entrance fee. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
key_features: discusses BOTH views with developed reasons (running costs, user pays, funding exhibitions vs access, repeat visits, public ownership)
clear personal opinion stated in the introduction and conclusion

model_answer.text:
Many museums and galleries charge visitors an entrance fee, while others are funded so that anyone can walk in without paying. Both approaches have serious arguments behind them, but I believe that, wherever possible, permanent collections should be free.

Those who support charging point out that museums are expensive to run. Buildings must be heated, lit and secured, and fragile objects need constant expert care. If visitors pay, the cost falls mainly on the people who actually use the service rather than on every taxpayer, including those who never visit. A fee may also encourage people to value the experience more, and the income can fund new exhibitions, educational programmes and research that would otherwise be impossible.

On the other hand, free entry has powerful social benefits. A museum is one of the few places where a family on a low income can show their children dinosaur skeletons, ancient tools or great paintings, and even a modest charge can make that visit unaffordable for a family of five. Free entry also encourages short, repeated visits: someone who has paid may feel obliged to see everything at once, whereas someone who can walk in freely can return many times to explore one gallery in depth. Moreover, most national collections were built up with public money or donations intended for the whole nation, so it seems fair that the public should be able to see them.

In my view, the best solution is a mixed model. The permanent collection should be free, funded by government grants, while special temporary exhibitions, which are costly to borrow and insure, can reasonably charge a fee. In this way, museums can raise extra income without excluding anyone from their basic cultural heritage.

In conclusion, although charging can help museums cover their costs, the educational and social value of open access is greater, so core collections should remain free to all.
